passage:
"Papa! Papa!" Kamal, two, screamed from his bed.

Dhruv ran in. "I'm here. What happened?"

Kamal pointed at the wall. "Big man!"

"That's the shadow of your coat, see?" Dhruv moved the coat. "Gone."

"Scary noise!"

"That's the neighbour's fan. Whirr, whirr."

Dhruv switched on the little star lamp and lay beside him. "I'm right here." Kamal held his thumb and slowly closed his eyes.

qa.q: What was making the big shadow on the wall?
qa.a: It was the shadow of Kamal's coat.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he screamed and pointed at the wall?
qa.a: Kamal felt terrified, because the shadow seemed real and big to him.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped Kamal feel safe?
qa.a: He came quickly, explained the shadow and the noise calmly, switched on the star lamp and stayed close, without mocking or threatening.

qa.q: What would change if Dhruv had said a ghost would come if Kamal didn't sleep?
qa.a: Kamal would become even more frightened of the dark and less able to settle.

grounding: Shows a toddler frightened by shadows and sounds at night and a parent who responds with a lamp, a calm voice and closeness.

passage:
Babysitter's note, Saturday.

Sabina, two, woke at ten, crying and pointing at the window. The curtain was moving in the breeze.

I didn't laugh. I switched on the night light, sat beside her and said softly, "It's the wind. You're safe." She clung to my arm.

I stayed until she slept. I told Thomas when he came home, and he said he'd put a heavier curtain up tomorrow.

qa.q: What was moving at the window?
qa.a: The curtain was moving in the breeze.

qa.q: Why did Sabina cling to the babysitter's arm?
qa.a: Sabina felt scared, because the moving curtain seemed frightening and real to her.

qa.q: Which steps by the babysitter helped Sabina?
qa.a: The babysitter didn't laugh, turned on the night light, spoke calmly and stayed close until she slept.

qa.q: How does Thomas respond when told about the night?
qa.a: Thomas takes it seriously and plans to put up a heavier curtain.

grounding: Shows a toddler afraid of a moving shape at night and a caregiver who responds with a night light, calm voice and closeness.

passage:
Health visitor's note, Monday.

Zeenat told me she shuts Simran, one and a half, in her room at bedtime and doesn't go in, however long she cries. "Now she's quiet after ten minutes," Zeenat said.

When I watched, Simran lay silent, staring, not calm. I sat with Zeenat and explained that Simran may be giving up, not settling.

We practised together: Zeenat sat by the cot, patted Simran and hummed. Simran cried, then slept holding her mother's hand. I will visit again Thursday.

qa.q: When will the health visitor visit again?
qa.a: The health visitor will visit again on Thursday.

qa.q: What might Simran's silent staring suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Simran felt overwhelmed and hopeless, having given up because crying brought no one.

qa.q: What did the health visitor do to help?
qa.a: The health visitor explained the silence gently, practised staying present with Zeenat, and planned a follow-up visit.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel after learning why Simran went quiet?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel surprised and guilty, but also relieved to have a warmer way to build sleep habits.

grounding: Shows a very young child who stops crying from giving up after being shut in alone, and a parent helped to respond warmly and stay present.

passage:
In their village house, Disha was exhausted after the harvest. Each night she closed the door on Kalyani, two, and went to the fields at dawn.

Kalyani's grandmother noticed. "She used to call for you. Now she just lies there, silent."

Disha went in. Kalyani's eyes were open, blank. Disha lay down beside her, humming. Kalyani grabbed her finger and cried hard, then slept.

After that, Disha stayed until she slept.

qa.q: What did Disha do after going into the room?
qa.a: Disha lay down beside Kalyani, humming.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she lay silent with blank eyes?
qa.a: Kalyani felt alone and had given up, not calm, after being left crying night after night.

qa.q: What changed that helped Kalyani?
qa.a: Disha began staying with her, humming until she slept, showing that someone would come.

qa.q: How does Kalyani's grandmother see the silence?
qa.a: The grandmother sees it as a worrying sign, not good behaviour, because Kalyani used to call out.

grounding: Shows a toddler going silent after being shut in alone, and a parent responding warmly and staying present at sleep time.

passage:
In their Helsinki bathroom, Aiko, two, sat on the potty and suddenly looked down, surprised.

"You did it!" Olga clapped. "In the potty!"

Aiko beamed and clapped too. "Did it!"

The next morning she had an accident on the rug. Olga just wiped it up. "Oops. We'll try again."

After breakfast Aiko marched to the potty by herself.

qa.q: Where did Aiko have an accident the next morning?
qa.a: Aiko had an accident on the rug.

qa.q: What does Aiko's beaming and clapping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Aiko felt proud and happy, glowing at her success.

qa.q: Why was Olga's response to the accident wise?
qa.a: Olga kept it calm and simple, without pressure, so Aiko stayed confident and tried again.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when Aiko marches to the potty alone?
qa.a: Olga likely feels delighted and proud, seeing that gentle cheer worked.

grounding: Shows a toddler beaming at warm, simple praise after a potty success, and a parent who ignores accidents kindly.

passage:
Monday. Tejas, two, used the potty for the first time. Vikas grinned. "Well done, Tejas!" Tejas clapped.

Wednesday. Two accidents. Vikas cleaned up without a word of blame. "No problem."

Two weeks later. Tejas ran to the potty, then shouted, "Papa, look!" Vikas gave him a high five. Tejas laughed and pulled up his shorts himself.

qa.q: What did Vikas give Tejas two weeks later?
qa.a: Vikas gave Tejas a high five.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he shouted "Papa, look!"?
qa.a: Tejas felt proud and excited to show his success.

qa.q: How did Vikas handle success and accidents?
qa.a: He praised success simply and warmly, and cleaned up accidents calmly without blame or pressure.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel after two weeks?
qa.a: Vikas likely feels pleased and patient, trusting Tejas's body to learn in its own time.

grounding: Shows a toddler who beams at simple praise after potty success, with accidents treated kindly over time.

passage:
"Uh-oh," said Kiran, two, standing in a puddle.

Uncle Pankaj laughed. "Chhee! Dirty girl!"

Kiran's face crumpled. She hid behind the curtain.

Her mother came with a cloth. "Pankaj, please don't. Kiran, it's okay. Accidents happen."

"Dirty," Kiran whispered.

"No, sweetheart. You're not dirty. We'll clean up and try the potty another day."

Kiran came out slowly and held her mother's hand.

qa.q: Where did Kiran hide?
qa.a: Kiran hid behind the curtain.

qa.q: Why did Kiran whisper "Dirty"?
qa.a: Kiran felt ashamed and embarrassed, believing her body was dirty after being laughed at.

qa.q: What did Kiran's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She stopped the laughing, cleaned up calmly, said accidents happen and planned to try another day.

qa.q: How might Uncle Pankaj have seen his joke, and how did Kiran experience it?
qa.a: Pankaj may have thought it was harmless fun, but Kiran experienced it as shaming and hid.

grounding: Shows a toddler shamed by laughter at a toileting accident, and a caregiver who cleans up calmly and says it is okay.

passage:
Creche note, Thursday.

At pickup, Neelam saw Ankita's wet clothes bag and said loudly, "Again? Bad girl!" Ankita, two, hung her head and hid behind my legs.

I spoke with Neelam quietly outside. I explained that scolding can make children hide accidents.

Neelam knelt. "It's okay, Ankita. We'll try again tomorrow." Ankita slowly came out and let her mother pick her up.

qa.q: What did Neelam see at pickup?
qa.a: Neelam saw Ankita's wet clothes bag.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she hung her head and hid?
qa.a: Ankita felt ashamed and scared after being called a bad girl.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do, and why did it help?
qa.a: The note-writer spoke with Neelam privately and explained how scolding can make children hide accidents, so Neelam reassured Ankita instead.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel after the quiet talk?
qa.a: Neelam may feel a little embarrassed, but also willing to respond more gently.

grounding: Shows a toddler shamed by scolding over accidents and a caregiver who helps the parent respond calmly instead.

passage:
In their small house in Thrissur, Joseph held out the potty. "Sudha, sit, please."

Sudha, two, shook her head, crossed her arms and squeezed her legs together.

"Sit now," Joseph said again. Sudha screamed.

Joseph stopped. "Okay. Want the blue potty or the red one?" Sudha pointed to the red one, but didn't sit.

"Maybe tomorrow," Joseph said, and put it away for a week.

qa.q: Which potty did Sudha point to?
qa.a: Sudha pointed to the red one.

qa.q: Why did Sudha cross her arms and squeeze her legs?
qa.a: Sudha felt determined to control her own body, and the pressure made her more stubborn.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that eased the struggle?
qa.a: Joseph stopped pushing, offered a choice, and put the potty away for a while when she wasn't ready.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Sudha screams?
qa.a: Joseph probably feels frustrated and worried, but he realises pushing is making it worse.

grounding: Shows a toddler refusing the potty to claim control, and a parent who drops the pressure, offers choices and pauses.

passage:
In their Oslo flat, Astrid set out the potty. Elif, two, looked at it and said, "No!"

Astrid shrugged calmly. "Okay. Do you want to read a book on it, or just sit with clothes on?"

Elif sat with her clothes on, reading about bears.

After three days of refusing, Astrid put the potty away. "We'll try next month." Elif waved it goodbye.

qa.q: What was Elif reading about?
qa.a: Elif was reading about bears.

qa.q: What does Elif's firm "No!" suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Elif felt stubborn and determined, wanting control over her own body.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Astrid to pause for a month?
qa.a: Pressure would sharpen Elif's resistance, and pausing when a child isn't ready keeps it low-key.

qa.q: How might Elif feel when the potty is put away?
qa.a: Elif likely feels relieved and in control, even cheerful, waving it goodbye.

grounding: Shows a toddler refusing the potty to claim control and a parent who keeps it low-key, offers choices and pauses.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday.

Nirmala, two, arrived watching videos on her grandfather Ramesh's phone. She stared, not blinking. When he took it, she screamed and hit the floor.

I offered sand and water play. At first she wailed. Then she dug.

I told Ramesh gently that short screen time, watched together, is kinder. He said he'd try more walks to the park instead.

qa.q: What did Ramesh say he'd try instead of the phone?
qa.a: Ramesh said he'd try more walks to the park.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's screaming when the phone was taken suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Nirmala felt upset and frustrated, her attention caught so strongly that losing the phone felt overwhelming.

qa.q: What did the note-writer offer instead of the screen?
qa.a: The note-writer offered hands-on sand and water play and advised shorter, shared screen time.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see the phone after the talk?
qa.a: Ramesh may now see it as something to limit and share, and look for outdoor time instead.

grounding: Shows a toddler stuck on a phone screen who screams when it is taken, and caregivers limiting it and offering hands-on and outdoor play.

passage:
On the charpai outside, Salma, two, held her mother Aparna's phone, face lit by fast cartoons. She didn't hear the goats or her cousins.

When Aparna took the phone, Salma screamed and kicked.

Aparna stayed calm. "Come, let's feed the goat." She carried her to the pen.

Salma sniffled, then giggled as the goat nibbled grass from her hand.

qa.q: What did Aparna take Salma to feed?
qa.a: Aparna took Salma to feed the goat.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when she screamed and kicked?
qa.a: Salma felt frustrated and upset, because the fast cartoons had held her attention completely.

qa.q: What did Aparna do that helped?
qa.a: She stayed calm, limited the phone, and offered a hands-on outdoor activity.

qa.q: How might Salma's cousins see her staring at the phone?
qa.a: The cousins might feel ignored, since she didn't hear them.

grounding: Shows a toddler absorbed in a phone who screams when it is taken, and a caregiver who limits it and offers outdoor play.

passage:
"Show done, Gopika," Kavitha said, switching off the TV.

Gopika, two, threw herself on the floor, kicking. "No! More!"

Kavitha sat beside her. "You're sad it's over. I know."

"More!"

"No more today." Kavitha opened her arms. "Hug?"

Gopika crawled in, sobbing. After a minute Kavitha said, "Shall we blow bubbles?" Gopika nodded, still sniffing.

qa.q: What did Kavitha suggest after the hug?
qa.a: Kavitha suggested blowing bubbles.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she threw herself on the floor?
qa.a: Gopika felt sad and frustrated that the show had ended.

qa.q: How did Kavitha hold the limit without anger?
qa.a: She stayed calm, named Gopika's sadness, kept the TV off, offered a hug and then a new activity.

qa.q: What might Kavitha be feeling while sitting on the floor with Gopika?
qa.a: Kavitha probably feels patient but tired, determined to stay calm and kind.

grounding: Shows a toddler's floor tantrum when the screen goes off, met by a calm parent who holds the limit, offers a hug and a new activity.

passage:
Babysitter's note, Sunday.

At four, I turned off the tablet. Trisha, two, dropped to the floor and wailed.

I didn't scold her. I sat close and said, "You wanted more. It's hard." She cried for a few minutes, then crawled onto my lap.

We made a tower of cups. She laughed when it fell.

— Usha

qa.q: What did Trisha and Usha build together?
qa.a: They made a tower of cups.

qa.q: What does Trisha dropping to the floor and wailing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Trisha felt sad and frustrated, not rude, when the tablet went off.

qa.q: What did Usha do that helped Trisha calm down?
qa.a: Usha stayed calm, named the feeling, held the limit, offered her lap and then a new activity.

qa.q: How might Usha feel when Trisha laughs at the falling tower?
qa.a: Usha likely feels relieved and warm, seeing the storm has passed and Trisha is happy again.

grounding: Shows a toddler's tantrum when the screen goes off, met by a caregiver who stays calm, holds the limit and offers comfort and play.

passage:
On the Mumbai local, Baljeet handed Nilesh, two, a phone full of cartoons to keep him quiet. Nilesh stared, silent.

At home, Baljeet sat on the sofa with his own phone. Nilesh held up a toy. No one looked.

That night Baljeet noticed Nilesh knew no new words. The next evening he left the phone aside and they named every car from the balcony. Nilesh chattered.

qa.q: What did Baljeet and Nilesh name from the balcony?
qa.a: They named every car from the balcony.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have been feeling when no one looked at his toy?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt lonely and ignored, wanting a person to share with.

qa.q: What did Baljeet change, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He put the phone aside and talked and played with Nilesh, treating the screen as a tool, not a babysitter.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have felt on noticing Nilesh knew no new words?
qa.a: Baljeet probably felt worried and a little guilty, realising the phone had replaced time together.

grounding: Shows a toddler given a phone instead of a person and a parent who begins talking and playing daily.

passage:
"Mumma, see!" Dilnaz, two, held up a leaf.

Deepika, typing, handed her the tablet. "Watch this, baby. Mumma's busy."

Dilnaz watched, silent, for an hour.

At bedtime, Dilnaz asked, "Mumma, play?"

Deepika paused. "Tomorrow, first thing, we'll play. No tablet."

Next morning they collected leaves in the park. Dilnaz talked the whole way.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz hold up to show her mother?
qa.a: Dilnaz held up a leaf.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz ask "Mumma, play?" at bedtime?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt lonely and wanted her mother's company, not just the tablet.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that helped?
qa.a: She made time the next morning to play with Dilnaz without the tablet, treating it as a tool, not a babysitter.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when Dilnaz asks to play?
qa.a: Deepika may feel a pang of guilt and realise Dilnaz needs her, not the screen.

grounding: Shows a toddler handed a tablet instead of attention and a parent who chooses daily play and talk.

passage:
On the village lane, a dog barked and leapt near Vishal, two. Vishal froze, then ran screaming to his uncle Sumit.

Sumit scooped him up and stepped back. "I've got you. The dog is loud."

They watched from the doorstep. After a while Vishal pointed. "Doggy."

"Yes, doggy. Sleeping now."

Sumit didn't carry him closer.

qa.q: Who did Vishal run to?
qa.a: Vishal ran to his uncle Sumit.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he froze?
qa.a: Vishal felt terrified by the barking, leaping dog.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Sumit not to carry him closer?
qa.a: Keeping a safe distance and not forcing contact lets Vishal's curiosity return slowly.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel seeing Vishal point at the dog later?
qa.a: Sumit likely feels relieved and glad that Vishal is becoming curious instead of frightened.

grounding: Shows a toddler terrified by a barking dog, comforted at a safe distance and allowed to become curious slowly.

passage:
In the Berlin park, a big dog bounded towards Jin, two. Jin shrieked and grabbed Fatima's legs.

Fatima picked her up. "You're safe. That dog is very jumpy." The owner called the dog back.

They sat on a bench and watched the dog play. Jin peeked out.

"Want to touch?" the owner asked.

"Not today," Fatima said.

qa.q: Where did Fatima and Jin sit to watch the dog?
qa.a: They sat on a bench.

qa.q: What does Jin grabbing Fatima's legs suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Jin felt frightened and wanted the safety of her parent.

qa.q: Why did Fatima say "Not today"?
qa.a: Fatima wanted Jin's curiosity to come back slowly without forcing touch.

qa.q: How might the dog's owner see the moment?
qa.a: The owner probably meant well, offering a touch, but Fatima's answer shows Jin needs more time.

grounding: Shows a toddler frightened by a bounding dog, comforted at a distance without being forced to touch.

passage:
"Moo!" Dhruv, two, pointed at the cow by the gate.

"Yes, moo!" said his sister Noor. "Want to give her grass?"

Dhruv grabbed at the cow's ear.

"Gentle hands," Noor said, holding his wrist softly. "Like this." She stroked the cow's neck.

Dhruv copied, stroking slowly. He giggled. "Moo!"

Noor kept her arm around him.

qa.q: Where was the cow standing?
qa.a: The cow was standing by the gate.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling as he giggled and said "Moo!"?
qa.a: Dhruv felt delighted and excited, wanting to touch the cow.

qa.q: How did Noor help Dhruv be safe with the cow?
qa.a: Noor modelled gentle hands, guided his wrist and stayed close with her arm around him.

qa.q: What might the cow experience when Dhruv grabs her ear?
qa.a: The cow might feel startled or uncomfortable, which is why gentle stroking is safer.

grounding: Shows a toddler delighted by a cow, with a caregiver modelling gentle hands and staying close.

passage:
Grandfather's note, Sunday.

Pranav, two, saw our calf and laughed, pointing. "Maa-maa!" He wanted to feed it.

I held his hand, put a little hay in his palm and showed him how to hold it flat. The calf licked it, and he squealed.

I kept him close, because the calf kicks sometimes.

— Ramesh

qa.q: What did Ramesh put in Pranav's palm?
qa.a: Ramesh put a little hay in Pranav's palm.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when the calf licked his hand?
qa.a: Pranav felt excited and delighted, squealing with joy.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh keep Pranav close?
qa.a: Ramesh knew the calf kicks sometimes, and a toddler cannot judge when an animal is unsafe.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel watching Pranav with the calf?
qa.a: Ramesh likely feels happy and proud, but also watchful for safety.

grounding: Shows a toddler delighted to feed a calf, with a grandfather modelling gentle handling and staying close for safety.
